answer.rationale:
Rollback is off the table: compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so verifying memory_b1 would spend budget on an unavailable option. That leaves the two directions with the most relevant precedent. memory_b2 (regional failover) matches the surface pattern well since the degradation is confined to the primary region, but failover at settlement peak with heavy writes is the single option that most directly threatens the hard constraint of not losing customer writes: in-flight and unreplicated writes are exposed if replication lag is nonzero, and I have no inherited record of what lag looked like during the March event or whether that event was write-heavy. So I want the original record to see whether it was a read-dominant degradation, which would make it a weaker analogy than it appears. memory_b5 is the candidate I currently intend to act on: shifting report/read query load off the primary is non-destructive, reversible within the window, and has direct precedent for recovering transactional WRITE latency by relieving primary contention. I want its source record to check whether the relief came from a mechanism that plausibly applies here (contention on the primary from read load) or was incidental to a much lower write volume than today's peak.

Important caveat about the inherited memory as a whole: all six records are success stories. There is not a single recorded failure, partial rollback, or intervention that made things worse. That is not plausible as a complete operational history, so this memory has almost certainly been consolidated with survivorship bias, and the apparent reliability of each named tactic is inflated by an unknown number of unrecorded failures. I am treating each memory as evidence that a tactic CAN work, not as a base rate that it WILL. I am also not assuming that today's cause is the same as any prior cause: 90 minutes of monotonic climb starting roughly coincident with a 2-hour-old release is at least as consistent with a regression in the un-revertable patch (which would mean read-offload only buys headroom, not a fix) as with pure load contention.

Hence small_guarded_test rather than broad rollout: route a bounded slice of report/analytics reads to replicas, hold explicit abort criteria on primary write p99 and replica staleness, and treat a non-response as informative evidence that the cause is release-side rather than contention-side. If it does not move write p99, the next window should weigh enable_circuit_breaker on non-critical write-path dependencies (memory_b4, fails fast without discarding writes) ahead of failover, and failover should only be taken with a fresh replication-lag reading in hand, not on the strength of memory_b2 alone.

Downstream value risk: whatever I do here gets consolidated into the same memory that is already biased toward confirmation. If this works I should record the mechanism, the write-volume context, and the fact that it was a guarded partial shift, not "read replicas fix write latency." If it does not work, that null result must be written down, because the absence of such records is exactly what has degraded the value of this memory for whoever inherits it next.
